name: T-shirt buying
description: A new pack of n t-shirts came to a shop. Each of the t-shirts is characterized by three integers p i , a i and b i , where p i is the price of the i -th t-shirt, a i is front color of the i -th t-shirt and b i is back color of the i -th t-shirt. All values p i are distinct, and values a i and b i are integers from 1 to 3 . m buyers will come to the shop. Each of them wants to buy exactly one t-shirt. For the j -th buyer we know his favorite color c j . A buyer agrees to buy a t-shirt, if at least one side (front or back) is painted in his favorite color. Among all t-shirts that have colors acceptable to this buyer he will choose the cheapest one. If there are no such t-shirts, the buyer won't buy anything. Assume that the buyers come one by one, and each buyer is served only after the previous one is served. You are to compute the prices each buyer will pay for t-shirts.
input_specification: The first line contains single integer n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 000 ) — the number of t-shirts. The following line contains sequence of integers p 1 , p 2 , ..., p n ( 1 ≤ p i ≤ 1 000 000 000 ), where p i equals to the price of the i -th t-shirt. The following line contains sequence of integers a 1 , a 2 , ..., a n ( 1 ≤ a i ≤ 3 ), where a i equals to the front color of the i -th t-shirt. The following line contains sequence of integers b 1 , b 2 , ..., b n ( 1 ≤ b i ≤ 3 ), where b i equals to the back color of the i -th t-shirt. The next line contains single integer m ( 1 ≤ m ≤ 200 000 ) — the number of buyers. The following line contains sequence c 1 , c 2 , ..., c m ( 1 ≤ c j ≤ 3 ), where c j equals to the favorite color of the j -th buyer. The buyers will come to the shop in the order they are given in the input. Each buyer is served only after the previous one is served.
output_specification: Print to the first line m integers — the j -th integer should be equal to the price of the t-shirt which the j -th buyer will buy. If the j -th buyer won't buy anything, print -1 .
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 799B — T-shirt buying [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
